https://www.politico.eu/article/germany-.text: BRUSSELS — The prospect of the far right running a German state for the first time since 1945 will provide the clearest warning yet to EU governments about the urgency of striking a deal on the bloc’s next seven-year budget. Sunday’s regional election in Saxony-Anhalt is giving European diplomats cause to sound the alarm over how disagreements between countries will only get worse next year. With 2027 set to see votes in France, Spain, Italy, Poland, Greece, Estonia and Slovakia, the prospect of other Euroskeptic voices sweeping to power — with a mandate to make the EU less expensive and less powerful — is focusing minds on getting a deal on the budget before the end of the year, four diplomats and officials told POLITICO. With its mix of nationalism and anti-migration rhetoric, the Alternative for Germany (AfD) is on course to be within a few seats of winning an absolute parliamentary majority in the east German state on Sunday. While that won’t directly change the country’s national leadership, votes in other countries next year might. Advertisement Advertisement “With four of the five largest EU member states voting in parliamentary or presidential elections, it will be more difficult to reach an agreement, especially if we look at the rise of anti-European populism,” said Siegfried Mureșan, the Parliament’s lead lawmaker on the budget. “Everyone understands the obvious negative consequences of a delayed adoption and entry into force of the MFF [the Multiannual Financial Framework, the seven-year budget].” Negotiations on the budget — which must be agreed by all 27 governments — have been deadlocked for months. Neither of the two main groups of countries, those that want the EU to have more to spend and those that want it to have less, has seen an advantage in giving ground so far. European Council President António Costa is currently touring capitals in an effort to narrow differences. “Saxony-Anhalt could really define the fall,” said one of those diplomats involved in the talks. “It will make it clear that it is crucial to get agreement this year. If we don’t get it in December, it can’t be February or March, that will be too close to the French election.” Alternative for Germany politician Ulrich Siegmund attends an event ahead of elections in Saxony-Anhalt, in Weißenfels on July 26, 2026. | Jens Schlueter/Getty Images Brussels is spooked by the prospect of France’s far-right veteran Marine Le Pen winning the country’s presidential election, scheduled to start on April 18, and following through on her campaign pledge to halve France’s contribution to the EU budget, the diplomats and EU officials said. Macron’s challenge But while at the European level that adds urgency for France to get a deal before the election, domestic pressures make it more complicated. Macron, whose far-right opponents are pushing for massive reductions in the country’s own EU contributions, is under pressure to get a deal that won’t worsen Paris’ national economic woes. He is pushing for new EU-wide taxes, known as “own resources,” as a way to pay for the bloc’s priorities without capitals being stuck with the bill themselves. France wants to give Brussels the power to put levies on U.S. digital giants, foreign polluters and online gambling. “Any agreement without own resources will be a no-go for France,” said an EU official. “We get it.” Advertisement Advertisement The disagreements got another airing at a meeting of European ministers which kicked off on Thursday in Ireland, which holds the six-month rotating presidency of the Council of the EU. Germany is leading a group of countries that want the EU budget to be smaller than that proposed by the European Commission, but any cuts will hit the very areas Brussels most wants to strengthen — competitiveness, defense and security — EU Budget Commissioner Piotr Serafin told reporters on the sidelines of the meeting. Those top priorities could “become the first victims of cuts,” he said. The budget will be discussed at a summit of EU leaders on Oct. 15, where Ireland will present an updated negotiating position. An additional summit is expected to be held Nov. 26-27, two officials confirmed, to advance the talks and a final, potentially very long, meeting will take place in December, where leaders will be persuaded not to leave without striking a deal, they said. ‘Difficult choices’ Countries are still split on the scale of the budget, with a handful of wealthier countries led by Germany pushing for hundreds of billions of euros to be shaved off the seven-year spending plan. Others, including Romania, Poland and other net recipients of EU funds, want to maintain the size of the pot. Meanwhile, the EU’s frontier countries have launched a push for more funding to deal with Russia’s hybrid threats and shore up their economies. “The next EU budget will inevitably involve difficult choices. There will never be enough money for every priority,” Estonian Prime Minister Kirsten Michal said following a meeting with Costa last week. “But the choice should be clear: Europe cannot ask its eastern members to carry a growing security burden while funding priorities as if the world had not changed.” The deadlock, while profound, looks likely to be resolved by a flurry of talks for the rest of this year, those involved in the negotiations said. “Everybody seems to be aware of and committed to the end-of-year deadline,” said one of the officials. Costa’s “key message has been we need to get this deal over the line by then because of the context.” Asked whether elections — including in Saxony-Anhalt — were creating a sense of urgency in budget talks, Ireland’s Europe Minister Thomas Byrne, who is steering the negotiations on behalf of the EU presidency country, said Dublin had a simple agenda: “To get it done by the end of the year in order that the legislation can be passed next year.” Another diplomat, from a country that wants to see the budget to be smaller than that the Commission proposed, put it more bluntly: “If you want to do it, you have to do it within the next three months. After that, maybe the party is over for all of us.” Advertisement Advertisement

Prices have spiked as a result of the US war with Iran, which has disrupted oil supplies through the Strait of Hormuz waterway, but Mr Trump has increasingly sought to lay the blame on attacks by Ukraine on Russian refineries. Photograph: Patrícia de Melo Moreira/AFP/Getty Images Opinion Portugal As housing protests sweep Portugal, police and politicians here seem bent on making the crisis worse Ana Naomi de Sousa While Spain, Germany and the UK have all introduced laws protecting renters’ rights, Luís Montenegro’s centre-right government is empowering landlords Fri 13 Nov 2026 00.00 EST Last modified on Fri 13 Nov 2026 05.29 EST Share A s Storm Charles reached Portugal’s shores this week, flights were aborted, schools were closed, and the global Web Summit in Lisbon was forced to cancel a whole day of lucrative events. But even the promise of some very bad weather was not enough to deter housing protesters from setting up camp for another night on the streets. Since 14 October, echoing recent eruptions over housing in Spain, and the fierce student-led protests in France , Lisbon and Porto have become the focus for encampments and daily protests drawing people in their thousands. Almost one month later, they show no sign of disappearing. The breadth of these demonstrations is as wide as the housing crisis that has provoked them. At the protests you might find architects, waiting staff, high school graduates, philosophers, young mothers, professional politicians, projectionists, security guards, graphic designers and master’s students. I met thirtysomething professionals still living with their parents, separated couples having to sleep under the same roof, and families torn between cramped living conditions in the city and moving far away from their jobs, schools and communities. On the days I spent at the protest camps, the mood was both animated and serious. There was a “people’s university”, a canteen serving free meals and people dropping by after work, university or school. A number of discrete social and housing movements from both cities have joined together. Some have come out to protest against their appalling living conditions, others are fighting eviction orders, and many more have found it impossible to move on with their lives because they can’t move home. In Paris they burned cars, while in Barcelona they built barricades; in Portugal, the most provocative act of the encampment was a giant spooning sleepover . There were also clowns, a dedicated group of supportive “ camp mothers ”, singalongs , and performances from pop singers Mayra Andrade and Ana Moura . The government’s responses have only made matters worse, ranging from the farcical to the outright repressive. Prime minister Luís Montenegro called the demonstrations “selfish”, and suggested they were a “foreign import”. Protesters have noted that he owns at least six properties across Portugal, as well as extensive land. Lisbon’s mayor, Carlos Moedas, complained about the impact protests would have on an upcoming German-style Christmas market. Meanwhile, the police reaction has been shocking and aggressive, with Lisbon’s police attacking peaceful protesters while they were sleeping . View image in fullscreen Housing protesters in Lisbon, 3 November 2026. Photograph: Ana Naomi de Sousa/The Guardian According to the Público newspaper more than 160 people have been injured – including some who were shot in the face with rubber bullets – and 99 arrested in Lisbon and Porto. Videos show police actively attacking protesters as they flee. The police brutality and impunity has provoked an outcry. More than 200 lawyers have signed a letter alleging disproportionate force and illegal measures, and demanding an inquiry. Amnesty International issued a statement accusing the police of “beatings and excessive force … causing physical harm and hospitalisations. This response is a choice. It can – and must – be stopped by the Portuguese authorities.” Why, then, is the government going to such lengths to avoid addressing what is one of Europe’s very worst housing crises? Access to decent, affordable housing has long been an issue that has afflicted low income – and, in particular, racialised – communities in Portugal; but it has become something that now affects even the professional middle classes. The numbers are so extreme, they seem impossible to ignore. Since 2015, house prices nationwide have increased by 169% ; in Porto, that figure rises to 180%; in Lisbon, it is 186% . Meanwhile, wage growth has failed to keep pace. Portugal has the highest discrepancy in the entire EU between house price and income . This state of crisis did not arrive overnight. The deregulation of Portugal’s housing market was set in motion following the 2011 bailout administered by the Troika (the European Commission, European Central Bank and International Monetary Fund) in the aftermath of a national financial crisis. The bailout conditions restricted government spending and borrowing, prompting the centre-right government at the time to seek new sources of private and foreign capital, making urban development increasingly dependent on private investment rather than public funding. It was also during this period that rental laws were relaxed to favour landlords, stoking a profit-driven rental market. Since then, huge swathes of land and property have become the target of speculation . A recent tourist boom has further inflated the profits being generated by property in Portugal. Tourism has become a significant driver of economic growth, but it has come at a different kind of cost. In Lisbon and Porto, the proliferation of short-term lets from sites like Airbnb has pushed rents and property prices up across dozens of neighbourhoods, forcing communities out as a consequence. Demonstrations about housing in Portugal have become increasingly frequent over the past five years, but have fallen on deaf ears. And while Spain, Germany and the UK have all recently implemented laws to protect renters’ rights, Portugal’s centre-right government is now introducing legislation to give greater powers to landlords to raise rents, demand larger deposits and evict tenants more quickly. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This is Europe The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment after newsletter promotion View image in fullscreen Housing protesters in Lisbon surround police attempting to fine motorists for tooting horns in support of the protest, 3 November 2026. Photograph: Ana Naomi de Sousa/The Guardian Since the protests began, Montenegro has made no signs of considering any concessions. His apparent public indifference has been accompanied by a series of attempts by elected officials to discredit and criminalise protesters. Moedas claimed that cleaning graffiti on Rossio square had cost the disputed sum of €138,000 (£115,000). Meanwhile, the police have been dreaming up some creative new means of repression; on 1 November they announced they would fine motorists €60 for tooting their horns in support of protesters – though they were forced to withdraw the measure within 24 hours. The response of Montenegro’s government can be understood in the context of Portugal’s current political tensions. Facing a serious challenge from the far-right Chega party , Montenegro’s Social Democratic party – a rightwing party, perhaps contrary to its name – is attempting to bring voters onboard through aggressive rhetoric around public policing and immigration. These bullying tactics are reminiscent of Portugal’s recent past. The chants frequently aimed at the police over the past month – “It reeks of dictatorship” (“ Cheira a ditadura ”), or “we are all anti-fascists” (“S omo todos anti-fascistas ”) – serve as a reminder that the country’s long imperial dictatorship (1926-1974) is still in living memory. But so is the spirit of resistance that eventually brought it crashing down. The Portuguese housing crisis isn’t going anywhere without radical interventions. The protesters in Portugal’s streets deserve more just and dignified solutions than to be ignored by politicians and beaten by police.
